description: We are a team of passionate and enthusiastic students participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge at Thrissur. Our team, Power CE, is interested in space science, technology, artificial intelligence, and innovative problem-solving.
summary: Flame in Free Fall is an SI-powered interactive dashboard designed to explore, analyze, and interpret NASA's microgravity combustion research. The platform brings together findings from space-based fire experiments to help users understand how flames behave in reduced-gravity environments. It summarizes and compares experimental results, identifies important fire-safety factors, and provides intelligent insights into flame behavior, fuel flammability, oxygen levels, airflow, and fire detection and suppression. By converting complex scientific data into accessible visualizations and actionable insights, the project aims to support safer spacecraft, space stations, lunar habitats, and future Mars missions. It also highlights how research in space can contribute to improved fire safety on Earth.
details:
Flame in Free Fall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

Our project, Flame in Free Fall, proposes an intelligent web-based research platform designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, understand and compare. In space, flames behave differently because the effects of gravity and natural convection are greatly reduced. Understanding these changes is essential for developing effective fire prevention, detection and suppression strategies for future space missions.

The platform provides a central interface to explore relevant NASA combustion investigations, including BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SAME, SAME-R, FLEX, FLEX-2 and other related experiments. Users can search investigations by name, research objective, fuel, material and experimental conditions. The proposed SI-powered features include automatic research summaries, relevance-based investigation ranking, comparison of experimental parameters and visual presentation of research information. Parameters of interest include fuel type, flame shape and size, oxygen concentration, airflow, experimental variations and sensor measurements.

The main benefit is to reduce the difficulty of finding and interpreting large volumes of scientific information. It aims to help students, researchers, professors and aerospace engineers identify relevant experiments and understand their contributions to spacecraft fire safety. Its intended impact is to support safer spacecraft, space stations, lunar habitats, pressurised rovers and future Mars missions. The research may also provide useful insights for fire-safety applications on Earth.

The website prototype was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTML provides the structure, CSS handles the visual design and responsive layout, and JavaScript supports search, filtering and interactive investigation details. The project is designed as a web-based software solution and does not require special hardware for its current prototype. NASA's Open Science Data Repository and Physical Sciences Informatics resources are considered reference sources for the research data.

The creative aspect of this project is the combination of space-combustion research with an intelligent, user-friendly data exploration approach. Instead of treating each experiment as isolated information, the platform aims to connect related investigations and make their findings easier to compare. Important factors considered include microgravity flame behavior, oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, fuel and material properties, airflow, detection methods, suppression techniques and the reliability of scientific sources.

The current website is a prototype with demonstration investigation records. Connecting verified NASA datasets and implementing the proposed SI-powered analysis features are planned development steps.
